p.x:
Today is my English exam. I woke up early and checked my bag. I have my ID card, my pencil case and a bottle of water.
My mum hugged me and said, "Good luck! Remember all your hard work." At school, my friends were nervous, but I felt calm.
In the exam, I read every question carefully. When I didn't know an answer, I made a guess. I tried to keep my writing neat and checked my spelling.
After the exam, my teacher smiled and said, "Well done! I'm sure you did your best." Now I'm waiting for the results.

After months of practice, exam day finally arrives. Here are some tips to help you do your best.
Before the exam, get a good night's sleep and eat breakfast. Arrive early, find the exam hall and check your seat number. Make sure you know the time limit for each part.
In the reading section, read the questions first and underline the keywords. Then you know what to look for in the text. In the writing section, plan your answer before you start. In the listening test, read the questions before the recording begins.
If a question is too difficult, don't give up. Move on and come back to it later. Remember that every point counts, and your effort matters more than being perfect.
When results day comes, you may be thrilled with your score, or you may feel disappointed. Either way, be proud of how far you have come. Many students who fail the first time pass with a much higher score on their second attempt. One exam is only one step on a long journey.

Successful candidates do not simply know more English; they understand how exams work. In the reading section, efficient readers rarely read every word. They first skim the passage to grasp its gist, then scan for specific information such as names, numbers or dates. Some questions test a precise detail, while others ask candidates to infer the writer's opinion or purpose from clues in the text rather than from direct statements.
In multiple-choice questions, a useful strategy is to eliminate options that are clearly wrong. Distractors are often designed to look attractive: they may contain words from the text but change their meaning, or they may be true in general but not according to the passage. Candidates who manage their time carefully are less likely to run out of time before the final section.
Writing tasks are usually assessed according to a mark scheme with several criteria, typically covering task achievement, organisation, vocabulary and grammar. An examiner will notice careless errors in punctuation, so it is essential to proofread your work and double-check the word count. Poor handwriting can also make an answer difficult to read.
Finally, attitude matters. Students who fall just below the pass mark or a grade boundary often feel devastated, but research on the growth mindset suggests that those who view failure as an opportunity to learn are far more likely to improve. Determination and self-belief help students bounce back from disappointment. For many people, retaking an exam and succeeding becomes a turning point, proof that persistence really does pay off.
